newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - States concerned about Food Stamp welfare changes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - States concerned about Food Stamp welfare changes.

text.p: It is lunchtime at the St. Francis of Assisi soup kitchen and hungry people are filing in -- twice the number of just a year ago. Because of the new federal welfare law there could soon be more.

"We've been running out of food," director Rosalind Williams said, attributing the increased need partly to cuts in state aid programs. Nearby, volunteers dish up steaming casserole in the scruffy basement of what, in better days, was a Roman Catholic grade school.

As Williams notifies her regulars of the kitchen's annual Thanksgiving meal, state officials are drafting a notice of their own, required under the welfare law, that could end Food Stamps for as many as 48,000 Pennsylvanians. By Nov. 22, six days before Thanksgiving, states must inform able-bodied Food Stamp recipients without children that they are limited to three months of federal food vouchers during any three-year period, unless they work 20 hours a week in a private job or government work and training programs.

It is part of the $28 billion in Food Stamp cuts that make up half the savings in the welfare law. Nationwide, a million people could lose benefits in an average month when the new work provision is in force, according to federal estimates.

"These are clearly the largest cuts ever made in the Food Stamp program," Robert Greenstein of the liberal Center on Budget and Policy Priorities said. The center estimates most people affected by the work provision get no government aid except Food Stamps. About half have no other income at all.

Republican lawmakers who wrote the provision say there is no reason for able-bodied people not to work, pointing to exceptions in the law for areas with high unemployment. They say Americans are fed up with abuse in the Food Stamp program.
"I hope the states would just not panic," Ohio Republican Rep. Robert Ney said. "Taxpayers would like able-bodied people to put some type of work into receiving Food Stamps."

As Nov. 22 approaches, some state governors are signaling they want relief. Three states have applied for waivers, allowed by the law, for areas with more than 10 percent unemployment. At least three others are preparing such requests, according to the U.S. Agriculture Department.

Pennsylvania Republican Gov. Tom Ridge, a supporter of the federal law, has pushed tough welfare changes through his state, but he wants the widest possible exception to protect some of the $39 million of Food Stamp funds at risk here.

"It was not so much philosophical as pragmatic," Tim Reeves, the governor's spokesman, said. If the state is forced to spend time and money finding jobs for Food Stamp recipients it could hamper efforts to move tens of thousands of welfare mothers to work as required under welfare reform.

Washington is late issuing guidelines for states like Pennsylvania that do not have high unemployment but want relief for regions where jobs are scarce. Frustrated state officials are debating whether to delay the notice and, if not, what to tell people like William Vazquez-Colon, 49.

Hunched over a long table at St. Francis, Vazquez-Colon reels off the address of every free pantry and soup kitchen in Harrisburg. He worked nearly two decades at an elevator plant but the past few years have been a series of temporary jobs.

"Jobs are not that plentiful. Most of the time they are low paying or part-time without benefits," he said. He has applied for work in fast-food restaurants, warehouses and other low-skilled industries.

Vazquez-Colon lost his $120-a-month Food Stamp benefit because of a technical glitch. He is reapplying but now has no income and depends on charity for his meals in a state where the overall unemployment rate is only five percent.

Recent studies have shown poor workers may face long periods of joblessness even in states with low unemployment as the number of low-skilled jobs shrinks. In nearby Philadelphia, which has actually lost jobs in recent years, 17,900 people would be affected by the new work provision.
Pennsylvania, which does not run a workfare program, has 1.1 million Food Stamp recipients. Only 10 states had Food Stamp workfare programs in 1995.
